title: k-nearest neighbours
summary: k-nearest neighbours stores every training example and predicts by looking at the k closest ones: a majority vote for classes, an average for numbers. Small k gives a jagged, high-variance boundary; large k a blunt, high-bias one. Distances depend on units, so standardise features first, and in very high dimensions all distances start to look alike.
llm_link: Retrieval-augmented generation is nearest-neighbour search: documents become embedding vectors, the question becomes a vector, and a vector database returns the closest chunks (usually by cosine similarity, with approximate search) for the language model to read.
key_ideas: No training: kNN memorises the data. Prediction = find the k closest stored points.
Distance between feature vectors is usually the Euclidean norm ‖a − b‖.
Classification: majority vote of the k neighbours. Regression: their average.
k = 1 overfits (jagged boundary, high variance); very large k underfits (high bias). Choose k on validation data.
Standardise features so units do not decide the distance. Prediction cost grows with the data, and in high dimensions distances concentrate (the curse of dimensionality).

quiz.q: What does k-nearest neighbours learn during training?
options: Nothing beyond storing the training examples
The mean of each class only
quiz.explain: kNN is a 'lazy' method: all the work happens at prediction time, when the query is compared with every stored example.

quiz.q: Predict the result: with k = 3, a query's nearest neighbours have labels [cat, dog, cat]. What does kNN predict?
options: the label of the farthest point
quiz.explain: Majority vote: two cats against one dog. (Odd k avoids ties for two classes.)

quiz.q: Features are floor area in m² (40 to 200) and bedrooms (1 to 5). Without standardising, what happens?
options: Area dominates the distance, so bedrooms barely matter
quiz.explain: Differences in area are tens or hundreds; differences in bedrooms are a few. The squared differences in area swamp the others purely because of units.

quiz.q: You lower k from 15 to 1. What usually happens to training accuracy and to the decision boundary?
options: Training accuracy falls; the boundary gets smoother
Training accuracy rises (to 100% with no duplicate points); the boundary becomes jagged
quiz.explain: With k = 1 every training point is its own nearest neighbour, so training accuracy is perfect, but the boundary wraps around noise: high variance.

quiz.q: In a RAG system, which step is a nearest-neighbour search?
options: Finding the stored document chunks whose embeddings are closest to the question's embedding
quiz.explain: The vector database returns the top-k chunks by similarity (often cosine), usually with approximate nearest-neighbour indexes for speed.

problems.title: kNN classifier with plain Python
problems.prompt:
Write knn_predict(train_X, train_y, query, k): compute the distance from query to every training point, take the labels of the k closest, and return the most common one. A euclidean function is provided.

Tip: sorted(pairs) on a list of (distance, label) tuples sorts by distance first, and collections.Counter(labels).most_common(1)[0][0] gives the winning label.

tests.name: nearest wins with k = 1
tests.code:
X = [[0, 0], [10, 10]]; y = ['a', 'b']
assert knn_predict(X, y, [1, 1], 1) == 'a', 'with k = 1 the single closest point decides'

tests.name: majority vote
tests.code:
X = [[0, 0], [0, 1], [5, 5], [1, 0]]; y = ['red', 'red', 'blue', 'blue']
out = knn_predict(X, y, [0.2, 0.2], 3)
assert out == 'red', f'the 3 nearest are red, red, blue: expected red, got {out}'

tests.name: uses the k closest, not the first k
tests.code:
X = [[9, 9], [8, 8], [0, 0], [0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]]; y = ['far', 'far', 'near', 'near', 'near']
out = knn_predict(X, y, [0, 0], 3)
assert out == 'near', f'sort by distance before taking k; got {out}'

tests.name: large k becomes the overall majority
tests.code:
X = [[0, 0], [10, 0], [11, 0], [12, 0], [13, 0]]; y = ['a', 'b', 'b', 'b', 'b']
assert knn_predict(X, y, [0, 0], 5) == 'b', 'with k = all points, the most common class overall wins (high bias)'

problems.title: All distances at once with broadcasting (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
For many queries at once, loops get slow. Write pairwise_dist(Q, X) where Q has shape (m, d) and X has shape (n, d), returning an (m, n) array whose entry [i, j] is the distance from query i to point j.

Broadcasting trick: Q[:, None, :] has shape (m, 1, d) and X[None, :, :] has shape (1, n, d); subtracting them gives (m, n, d). Square, sum over the last axis, take the square root.

Then write knn_classify(Q, X, y, k) for integer labels 0/1 that returns one predicted label per query (use np.argsort along axis 1 and a mean of the neighbours' labels > 0.5).
